title: Concept of Temperature and Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
short_intro: Temperature is a macroscopic scalar physical property that quantitatively determines the thermal state of a system and dictates the direction of spontaneous net heat transfer. It originates microscopically from the average translational kinetic energy of the constituent particles.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of temperature, thermal equilibrium, empirical temperature scales (Celsius, Fahrenheit, Kelvin), principle of thermometry, and simple conversion relations.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics, kinetic interpretation of temperature using degrees of freedom, ideal gas temperature scale, absolute zero, and thermodynamic temperature scale based on Carnot engines.

prerequisites: Kinetic theory of gases and microscopic random motion
Degrees of freedom and the law of equipartition of energy

concept_notes.heading: Thermal Equilibrium and the Zeroth Law
bullets: Two systems are in thermal equilibrium if, when placed in thermal contact through a diathermal wall, their macroscopic properties do not change with time.
The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics states that if two systems A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system C, then they are also in thermal equilibrium with each other.
This law provides the logical foundation for the existence of temperature as a universal property shared by systems in thermal equilibrium.

concept_notes.heading: Microscopic Definition of Temperature
bullets: According to the kinetic theory of gases, the absolute temperature T of an ideal gas is directly proportional to the average translational kinetic energy per molecule.
Expressed via the equipartition theorem, each translational degree of freedom contributes (1/2)k<sub>B</sub>T to the internal energy per molecule.
Temperature measures the intensity of thermal agitation rather than the total thermal energy contained within the system.

concept_notes.heading: Empirical Temperature Scales
bullets: Temperature scales are constructed by choosing two reproducible fixed points, such as the ice point and the steam point of pure water at standard atmospheric pressure.
The Celsius scale defines the ice point as 0 degrees C and the steam point as 100 degrees C, divided into 100 equal intervals.
The Kelvin scale sets its zero at absolute zero (-273.15 degrees C) and uses the triple point of water (273.16 K) as its single defining fixed point.

concept_notes.heading: Thermodynamic Temperature Scale
bullets: The thermodynamic (Kelvin) scale is independent of the specific thermometric substance or property used to measure it.
It is defined using the efficiencies of reversible heat engines operating between two thermal reservoirs according to Kelvin's formulation.
Absolute zero (0 K) represents the theoretical limit at which the entropy of a pure crystalline substance vanishes, per the Third Law of Thermodynamics.

derivations.title: Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature
derivations.conditions: Ideal gas containing N molecules in volume V at absolute temperature T
steps: Start with the kinetic theory pressure relation for an ideal gas: P = (1/3)(Nm/V)(v_rms)^2
Substitute the ideal gas equation of state: PV = N k_B T, yielding (1/3)m(v_rms)^2 = k_B T
Multiply both sides by (3/2) to isolate the average translational kinetic energy per molecule: (1/2)m(v_rms)^2 = (3/2)k_B T
derivations.result: E_k = (3/2)k_B T, proving that temperature is a direct measure of average molecular kinetic energy.

derivations.title: Conversion Relation Between Celsius and Fahrenheit Scales
derivations.conditions: Standard linear thermometric scaling between ice point and steam point
steps: Establish the linear mapping equation: (C - C_ice)/(C_steam - C_ice) = (F - F_ice)/(F_steam - F_ice)
Substitute Celsius points (C_ice = 0, C_steam = 100) and Fahrenheit points (F_ice = 32, F_steam = 212)

graphs_and_experiments.title: Pressure vs Temperature Isochoric Plot for Gases
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Straight lines of P versus T for different constant volumes, intersecting the temperature axis at -273.15 C.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Extrapolation of all isochores to zero pressure yields a common temperature intercept of absolute zero (-273.15 C), establishing the absolute zero concept.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in conceptual MCQs regarding absolute zero and gas behavior.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Constant Volume Gas Thermometer Calibration Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Plot of measured gas pressure P against standard temperature T, showing a linear dependence.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirms Gay-Lussac's Law and shows that the extrapolated pressure vanishes at absolute zero Kelvin.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Basis of primary thermometry questions in PGT examinations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Triple Point Cell of Water
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic diagram showing solid ice, liquid water, and water vapor coexisting in equilibrium in a sealed glass cell.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Defines the exact thermodynamic fixed point (273.16 K, 611.65 Pa) for the Kelvin scale independent of atmospheric fluctuations.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Theoretical questions regarding modern definition of absolute temperature scale.

solved_numericals.question: At what temperature do the numerical values of the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales coincide?
solution_steps: Let the reading on both scales be x. Set C = x and F = x in the conversion formula.
Cross multiply and solve for x: 9x = 5(x - 32) -> 9x = 5x - 160 -> 4x = -160 -> x = -40

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the root mean square velocity of oxygen molecules (M = 32 g/mol) at a temperature of 27 degrees C. Take R = 8.314 J/(mol K).
solution_steps: Convert temperature to Kelvin: T = 27 + 273.15 = 300.15 K (or 300 K for approximation).
Convert molar mass to SI units: M = 32 x 10^-3 kg/mol.
Apply the formula v_rms = sqrt(3RT / M) = sqrt((3 x 8.314 x 300) / (32 x 10^-3)).
Compute value: sqrt(7482.6 / 0.032) = sqrt(233831.25) approx 483.5 m/s.

solved_numericals.question: A Carnot engine operates between reservoirs at 500 K and 300 K. If the source temperature is increased by 50 K while the sink temperature remains constant, find the percentage change in its efficiency.

assumptions_and_limitations: Temperature defined via the ideal gas equation is strictly valid only in the limit of zero pressure (ideal gas limit).
Real gases liquefy or solidify before reaching absolute zero, making absolute zero an asymptotic limit unattainable in finite steps (Third Law of Thermodynamics).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Temperature is a measure of the total heat energy contained in a body.
common_misconceptions.correct: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecular motion, not the total thermal energy.
common_misconceptions.why: A small cup of boiling water has a high temperature but less total thermal energy than a swimming pool filled with warm water.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Heat flows from a body with higher thermal energy to one with lower thermal energy.
common_misconceptions.correct: Heat flows spontaneously from a body at a higher temperature to one at a lower temperature.
common_misconceptions.why: Direction of heat transfer is strictly governed by temperature gradients, independent of the relative mass or total internal energy.

quick_revision: Temperature dictates the direction of spontaneous thermal energy flow and is quantified using empirical and thermodynamic scales.
